title: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering: Improving Imitation Learning Policy Robustness through Expert Hidden-State Geometry

paper.title: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering: Improving Imitation Learning Policy Robustness through Expert Hidden-State Geometry
paper.abstract:
Abstract Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy.
We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining.
Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions.
Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy.
DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space.
This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate.
Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies.
Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling.
Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Imitation learning (IL) trains robot policies from expert demonstrations, but the observations encountered during execution also depend on the policy’s own actions. Observation noise or action errors can therefore take the policy into conditions poorly represented in the demonstrations, where further errors can compound and disrupt task execution. DAgger addresses this distribution mismatch by obtaining expert actions on learner-visited states, while DART collects demonstrations that include recovery from disturbances [ 1 , 2 ] . Online reinforcement learning can also improve pretrained robot policies by updating their parameters using reward feedback from interaction [ 3 ] . These approaches all require information beyond the original demonstration set, such as new expert labels, additional demonstrations, or reward feedback from interaction. This motivates a complementary question: whether the original demonstrations alone can improve the closed-loop robustness of a trained IL policy without additional demonstrations or policy retraining. A neural IL policy processes observations into hidden states, which its later layers use to generate actions. Replaying the original demonstrations through the frozen policy exposes the hidden states associated with expert behavior, providing a policy-specific reference that can be reused during deployment without additional supervision. Intermediate hidden states therefore provide a natural intervention point: modifying one during execution can change the action while leaving the policy parameters fixed. We refer to this operation as test-time hidden-state steering . Prior work learns hidden-state correction modules jointly with the task network [ 4 ] , or steers trained robot policies using conceptors fitted to successful and failed roll-out activations [ 5 ] . In our demonstration-only setting, the steering reference instead consists solely of expert hidden states collected from the original demonstrations. The resulting challenge is how to use the structure of these expert hidden states to suppress undesirable deviations while preserving the variation needed for action generation. Our empirical analysis finds that expert hidden states vary predominantly within relatively few dimensions, while linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states differ in orientation (Section IV-A ). These observations motivate viewing the expert distribution as concentrated near a low-dimensional manifold, with broad variation along local tangent subspaces and narrow variation along local normal subspaces. Variation along this structure can reflect differences between demonstrated situations that require different actions. The steering problem can therefore be viewed as reducing departures from the structure while limiting changes to the variation needed for action generation. One way to pursue this goal is to attenuate components along directions with low expert variance more strongly than those along directions with high variance. A linear filter can implement this rule using globally fitted directions and attenuation factors [ 6 ] . Under the manifold view, however, local tangent and normal subspaces can change orientation with location. A fixed linear filter may therefore attenuate tangential expert variation as well as normal deviations, motivating steering directions that adapt to the local geometry. (b) A learned diffeomorphic chart maps hidden states to coordinates where DHS attenuates low-variance coordinates more strongly than high-variance coordinates while retaining every coordinate. (c) Mapping back through the inverse chart produces location-dependent hidden-state updates. Here, a i a_{i} is the fitted expert variance of chart coordinate i i , and β \beta controls steering strength. Our key idea is to use nonlinear expert coordinates for selective attenuation, limiting changes to high-variance coordinates while attenuating low-variance coordinates more strongly. We implement this idea with Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns a diffeomorphic coordinate map, or chart , from expert hidden states. DHS builds on score-based pullback Riemannian geometry (SPRG) [ 7 ] to learn the chart and an anisotropic Gaussian model of expert variation in its coordinates. Under the manifold view, high and low-variance coordinates serve as proxies for tangential variation and normal deviations, respectively. The inverse chart provides location-dependent coordinate directions for selective attenuation in hidden-state space. At test time, DHS maps the current hidden state to chart coordinates, rescales them according to their fitted expert variances, and maps the result back before the remaining policy layers generate an action (Fig. 1 ). Our contributions are as follows: • We characterize expert hidden-state geometry in a trained IL policy, observing concentrated variation and differences in the orientation of linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states. • We introduce DHS, a full-rank nonlinear steering operator that uses expert hidden-state geometry to attenuate low-variance chart coordinates while limiting changes to high-variance coordinates in a frozen IL policy. • We demonstrate that DHS achieves higher mean success than the unmodified policy under observation noise across four simulated manipulation tasks. Also, learned nonlinear coordinates yield higher mean success than linear coordinates from principal component analysis (PCA) under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling.

sections.heading: II-A Hidden-State Steering and Filtering
sections.text: Hidden-state steering can be learned jointly with a task network or derived from the statistics of reference activations. State-Reification Networks jointly train denoising or attractor modules with the task network to improve generalization, and combine state reification with adversarial training to improve adversarial robustness [ 4 ] . The statistical approach underlies conceptor filters, which use second moments of recurrent activity to preserve characteristic patterns and control their generation [ 6 ] . COAST applies this principle to robot policies by combining conceptors fitted to successful and failed roll-out activations [ 5 ] . Each fitted conceptor applies a linear map in hidden-state space. DHS uses nonlinear expert coordinates whose induced coordinate basis can vary with the current hidden state, allowing variance-dependent steering to follow the learned geometry.

sections.heading: II-B Representation Geometry and Nonlinear Steering
sections.text: Studies of intrinsic dimension in image classification networks [ 8 ] and representation geometry in protein and image Transformers [ 9 ] motivate examining how expert variation is organized within robot policies. A constructive approach to such geometry is provided in [ 7 ] : anisotropic flows yield tractable pullback geometry and a Riemannian autoencoder that reconstructs data after retaining high-variance coordinates. DHS builds on this coordinate construction for full-rank selective attenuation during policy execution. Geometry also affects how interventions move between represented behaviors. Interpolation along fitted activation manifolds is examined in Manifold Steering through behavioral transitions in structured language tasks and a visual world model [ 10 ] . For targeted behavioral changes, Curveball Steering applies contrastive shifts in polynomial kernel PCA coordinates, using approximate inversion and restoring the reconstruction residual [ 11 ] . These approaches establish precedents for nonlinear geometric intervention; our focus is how expert variation can guide corrective attenuation steering while preserving execution of an existing robot task.

sections.heading: II-C Predictive Guidance and Activation Feedback
sections.text: Guidance can also be derived from an action’s predicted consequences. Proximity to expert observation embeddings supplies the objective in Latent Policy Barrier, where dynamics learned from expert data and policy roll-outs guide action denoising through predicted future embeddings [ 12 ] . Predicted future state values provide another criterion: Cosmos Policy learns action, state, and value predictions by fine-tuning a video model, and uses these values to select action proposals in its planning mode [ 13 ] . Feedback can instead operate across network depth, as in WA-LQR, which locally linearizes diffusion Transformer blocks to track contrastive robustness feature targets [ 14 ] . For DHS, the correction reference is the fitted distribution of expert hidden states: coordinate variances determine the attenuation directly, without future state prediction or contrastive feature tracking.

We seek to improve its closed-loop task success under observation noise by modifying an intermediate hidden state during execution, with all policy parameters θ \theta fixed. We select a single intermediate layer ℓ \ell and denote the hidden state to be modified at control step t t by h t ∈ ℝ d h_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , where d d is its dimension. sections.heading: IV-A Empirical Geometry of Expert Hidden States
sections.text: Studies of image classifiers and Transformers have reported evidence of low-dimensional manifold structure in hidden representations [ 8 , 9 ] . Motivated by these findings, we examine whether the expert hidden-state distribution from an IL robot policy is concentrated in relatively few dimensions and whether regional linear subspaces differ in orientation. We select the Square manipulation task from Robomimic [ 15 ] as a representative task and use a Transformer policy trained by behavior cloning (BC-Transformer). We analyze the approximately 27,000 expert hidden states that form ℋ E \mathcal{H}_{E} , obtained by replaying the original training demonstrations through the frozen policy. To quantify variance concentration, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the mean-centered states. We compute the cumulative explained variance as the sum of the leading covariance eigenvalues divided by the sum of all eigenvalues. Using the 90 % 90\% explained variance criterion employed in prior work [ 8 ] , we find that 29 principal components suffice in the ambient 512 dimensional space. Thus, most observed expert variation can be captured by a low-dimensional linear subspace. For a curved manifold, local tangent subspaces can change orientation relative to the fixed coordinate axes of the hidden-state space. To examine this possibility, we partition the same states into eight clusters using k k -means and fit a rank-29 PCA subspace within each cluster, using these regional subspaces as empirical proxies for local tangent subspaces. We compare every pair of PCA subspaces using principal angles, computed as the inverse cosines of the singular values of the matrix of inner products between their orthonormal basis vectors. Each pair yields 29 principal angles; all are zero for identical subspaces, while larger angles indicate greater differences in orientation. Averaging all 29 principal angles over all 28 cluster pairs gives 44.7 ∘ 44.7^{\circ} , indicating differences in the orientations of the fitted regional subspaces. Together, the variance concentration and regional orientation differences support a low-dimensional manifold-like view of expert hidden-state geometry. These observations therefore motivate the use of a nonlinear chart that allows coordinate rescaling to act along location-dependent directions in hidden-state space.

sections.heading: V-A Evaluation Setup
sections.text: We evaluate policies on four simulated manipulation tasks: Square, Transport, and Can from Robomimic [ 15 ] , and Coffee-D1 from MimicGen [ 17 ] (Fig. 2 ). For each task, all methods use the same frozen BC-Transformer checkpoint with low-dimensional observations. All hidden-state methods intervene on the final token at the same layer of the frozen policy. At each policy call, independent noise drawn from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) is added to every element of the observation history in its original feature units; overlapping observations are re-perturbed on subsequent calls. The protocol uses neither observation normalization nor quaternion renormalization. We compare DHS with alternatives fitted to expert hidden states at the same layer: PCA projection , autoencoder (AE) reconstruction , k k -nearest neighbor (kNN) replacement , and a Gaussian score step . These alternatives test linear truncation, nonlinear reconstruction, replacement by the mean of the k k nearest expert hidden states, and density-based correction in standardized hidden-state coordinates. At the action level, Action EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) combines recent action predictions with exponentially decaying weights, resetting between episodes. We evaluate it alone and in combination with DHS. The unmodified policy is denoted as no steering . Details are in Appendix B .

sections.heading: V-B Closed-Loop Success under Observation Noise
sections.text: We evaluate DHS and all baselines under observation noise with level σ \sigma . For each task, we choose a noise level that noticeably reduces the success rate of the no steering baseline relative to clean observations ( σ = 0 \sigma=0 ). The comparison in Table I uses three roll-out seeds with 100 episodes per seed and reports percent success as mean ± \pm sample standard deviation (SD) across seeds. Bold entries indicate the highest mean in each column. Policy and chart checkpoints remain fixed across seeds, so SD measures roll-out variability. The task-specific DHS strengths β \beta are selected by hyperparameter search and used unchanged for clean and noisy evaluations, both with and without Action EWMA. DHS improves mean noisy success over no steering on all four tasks in Table I , by 3.7 3.7 to 12.0 12.0 percentage points. It also achieves higher noisy means than the Gaussian score step on all four tasks and the highest noisy mean among the hidden-state methods on Square, Can, and Coffee-D1. To examine the role of coordinate choice, Section V-C compares linear and nonlinear coordinates under hard projection and full-rank rescaling. The interventions act at different stages: DHS adjusts the selected hidden-state before the current action is generated, while Action EWMA combines recent action predictions. Adding DHS to Action EWMA increases mean noisy success from 57.7 % 57.7\% to 61.7 % 61.7\% on Square and from 56.3 % 56.3\% to 62.0 % 62.0\% on Transport, yielding the highest noisy mean among the evaluated methods on both tasks. On Can and Coffee-D1, DHS alone achieves the highest noisy mean. The gains over Action EWMA on Square and Transport show that hidden-state steering can also benefit policies whose action outputs are already smoothed.

sections.heading: V-C Why Use Learned Nonlinear Coordinates?
sections.text: Section IV-A shows that 29 principal components explain 90% of the variance in expert hidden states on Square. We now ask whether learned nonlinear coordinates are more effective than linear PCA coordinates for hidden-state steering. We use Square as a representative task for this comparison under hard projection and full-rank rescaling, with PCA fitted to standardized expert hidden states. Both comparisons use three roll-out seeds with 100 episodes per seed; noisy evaluations use a noise level of σ = 0.05 \sigma{\,=\,}0.05 . First, we use 29 as a common retained dimension for PCA and the learned chart. For both PCA and the learned chart, we keep the 29 highest variance coordinates and set the remaining coordinates to zero. We map the modified coordinates back to a hidden state and insert it at the same intervention layer of the frozen policy. The learned chart yields higher mean success than PCA in both clean and noisy conditions (Table II ), showing that the choice of coordinates affects task success even when the same number of coordinates is retained. We next test whether the learned chart remains beneficial when all 512 coordinates are retained. We compare DHS with PCA-Wiener , which applies the same rescaling rule in the complete linear PCA basis using its empirical coordinate variances. For this comparison, each method’s strength is selected by mean development success and fixed before evaluation on disjoint seeds. Both methods use matching episode initializations and random seeds. DHS achieves higher mean noisy success, 50.3 ± 9.1 % 50.3\pm 9.1\% versus 44.0 ± 4.6 % 44.0\pm 4.6\% , reported as mean ± \pm sample SD across seeds (Table II ). The learned chart yields higher mean success under both update rules, supporting coordinate choice as an important component of effective hidden-state steering on Square. sections.heading: VI-A Expert Geometry as a Steering Reference
sections.text: DHS gives the original demonstrations a second role after policy training: their hidden states provide a reference for steering the frozen policy during execution. This separates policy training from the design of the steering update, without requiring additional expert action targets. The expert hidden-state density does not uniquely determine the update: different chart scales can describe the same density while yielding different DHS updates at a fixed β > 0 \beta>0 (Appendix A-C ). Chart learning and regularization therefore help define the steering rule, in addition to fitting the expert distribution.

sections.heading: VI-B Limitations
sections.text: DHS fits the distribution of expert hidden states, including their observation history information, without modeling temporal transitions. A hidden-state can be compatible with the fitted distribution yet inappropriate for the current task phase or a successful continuation. Combining expert geometry with predictions of an intervention’s future consequences is a natural extension, connecting hidden-state steering with predictive guidance [ 12 , 13 ] . The evaluation covers fixed BC-Transformer checkpoints with low-dimensional observations in simulation, and a single intervention site. In Table I , DHS reduces clean Transport success from 45.0 % 45.0\% to 36.0 % 36.0\% , and adding Action EWMA to DHS lowers noisy success on Can and Coffee-D1. The fitted geometry depends on preprocessing and chart regularization; its coordinate statistics provide a steering reference rather than a model of task error. Future work could also combine DHS with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection to adapt when and how strongly steering should be applied based on departures from the expert hidden-state distribution.

sections.heading: VII Conclusion
sections.text: DHS uses expert hidden-state geometry to improve the robustness of frozen IL policies at test time. Motivated by the low-dimensional manifold-like geometry of expert hidden states, its central idea is to apply variance-dependent rescaling in nonlinear coordinates to produce location-dependent steering directions. We use SPRG-based chart learning to fit expert coordinates and their variances. DHS improves mean success over the unmodified policy across four simulated manipulation tasks under observation noise. On Square, the learned coordinate construction yields higher mean success than linear PCA coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. The strength sweep further shows that stronger coordinate attenuation does not necessarily improve execution. Together with the gains over unmodified policies and the benefits alongside Action EWMA on Square and Transport, these results establish expert hidden states as a useful reference for selective test-time steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining.

Abstract Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy. We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining. Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions. Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy. DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space. This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies. Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone. I Introduction Imitation learning (IL) trains robot policies from expert demonstrations, but the observations encountered during execution also depend on the policy’s own actions. Observation noise or action errors can therefore take the policy into conditions poorly represented in the demonstrations, where further errors can compound and disrupt task execution. DAgger addresses this distribution mismatch by obtaining expert actions on learner-visited states, while DART collects demonstrations that include recovery from disturbances [ 1 , 2 ] . Online reinforcement learning can also improve pretrained robot policies by updating their parameters using reward feedback from interaction [ 3 ] . These approaches all require information beyond the original demonstration set, such as new expert labels, additional demonstrations, or reward feedback from interaction. This motivates a complementary question: whether the original demonstrations alone can improve the closed-loop robustness of a trained IL policy without additional demonstrations or policy retraining. A neural IL policy processes observations into hidden states, which its later layers use to generate actions. Replaying the original demonstrations through the frozen policy exposes the hidden states associated with expert behavior, providing a policy-specific reference that can be reused during deployment without additional supervision. Intermediate hidden states therefore provide a natural intervention point: modifying one during execution can change the action while leaving the policy parameters fixed. We refer to this operation as test-time hidden-state steering . Prior work learns hidden-state correction modules jointly with the task network [ 4 ] , or steers trained robot policies using conceptors fitted to successful and failed roll-out activations [ 5 ] . In our demonstration-only setting, the steering reference instead consists solely of expert hidden states collected from the original demonstrations. The resulting challenge is how to use the structure of these expert hidden states to suppress undesirable deviations while preserving the variation needed for action generation. Our empirical analysis finds that expert hidden states vary predominantly within relatively few dimensions, while linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states differ in orientation (Section IV-A ). These observations motivate viewing the expert distribution as concentrated near a low-dimensional manifold, with broad variation along local tangent subspaces and narrow variation along local normal subspaces. Variation along this structure can reflect differences between demonstrated situations that require different actions. The steering problem can therefore be viewed as reducing departures from the structure while limiting changes to the variation needed for action generation. One way to pursue this goal is to attenuate components along directions with low expert variance more strongly than those along directions with high variance. A linear filter can implement this rule using globally fitted directions and attenuation factors [ 6 ] . Under the manifold view, however, local tangent and normal subspaces can change orientation with location. A fixed linear filter may therefore attenuate tangential expert variation as well as normal deviations, motivating steering directions that adapt to the local geometry. Fig. 1: Schematic overview of DHS. (a) Expert hidden states are schematically shown near a curved structure; blue arrows indicate local tangent directions. (b) A learned diffeomorphic chart maps hidden states to coordinates where DHS attenuates low-variance coordinates more strongly than high-variance coordinates while retaining every coordinate. (c) Mapping back through the inverse chart produces location-dependent hidden-state updates. Gray points denote expert samples; open orange and filled blue markers indicate states before and after steering. Here, a i a_{i} is the fitted expert variance of chart coordinate i i , and β \beta controls steering strength. Our key idea is to use nonlinear expert coordinates for selective attenuation, limiting changes to high-variance coordinates while attenuating low-variance coordinates more strongly. We implement this idea with Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns a diffeomorphic coordinate map, or chart , from expert hidden states. DHS builds on score-based pullback Riemannian geometry (SPRG) [ 7 ] to learn the chart and an anisotropic Gaussian model of expert variation in its coordinates. Under the manifold view, high and low-variance coordinates serve as proxies for tangential variation and normal deviations, respectively. The inverse chart provides location-dependent coordinate directions for selective attenuation in hidden-state space. At test time, DHS maps the current hidden state to chart coordinates, rescales them according to their fitted expert variances, and maps the result back before the remaining policy layers generate an action (Fig. 1 ). Our contributions are as follows: • We characterize expert hidden-state geometry in a trained IL policy, observing concentrated variation and differences in the orientation of linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states. • We introduce DHS, a full-rank nonlinear steering operator that uses expert hidden-state geometry to attenuate low-variance chart coordinates while limiting changes to high-variance coordinates in a frozen IL policy. • We demonstrate that DHS achieves higher mean success than the unmodified policy under observation noise across four simulated manipulation tasks. Also, learned nonlinear coordinates yield higher mean success than linear coordinates from principal component analysis (PCA) under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. II Related Work II-A Hidden-State Steering and Filtering Hidden-state steering can be learned jointly with a task network or derived from the statistics of reference activations. State-Reification Networks jointly train denoising or attractor modules with the task network to improve generalization, and combine state reification with adversarial training to improve adversarial robustness [ 4 ] . The statistical approach underlies conceptor filters, which use second moments of recurrent activity to preserve characteristic patterns and control their generation [ 6 ] . COAST applies this principle to robot policies by combining conceptors fitted to successful and failed roll-out activations [ 5 ] . Each fitted conceptor applies a linear map in hidden-state space. DHS uses nonlinear expert coordinates whose induced coordinate basis can vary with the current hidden state, allowing variance-dependent steering to follow the learned geometry. II-B Representation Geometry and Nonlinear Steering Studies of intrinsic dimension in image classification networks [ 8 ] and representation geometry in protein and image Transformers [ 9 ] motivate examining how expert variation is organized within robot policies. A constructive approach to such geometry is provided in [ 7 ] : anisotropic flows yield tractable pullback geometry and a Riemannian autoencoder that reconstructs data after retaining high-variance coordinates. DHS builds on this coordinate construction for full-rank selective attenuation during policy execution. Geometry also affects how interventions move between represented behaviors. Interpolation along fitted activation manifolds is examined in Manifold Steering through behavioral transitions in structured language tasks and a visual world model [ 10 ] . For targeted behavioral changes, Curveball Steering applies contrastive shifts in polynomial kernel PCA coordinates, using approximate inversion and restoring the reconstruction residual [ 11 ] . These approaches establish precedents for nonlinear geometric intervention; our focus is how expert variation can guide corrective attenuation steering while preserving execution of an existing robot task. II-C Predictive Guidance and Activation Feedback Guidance can also be derived from an action’s predicted consequences. Proximity to expert observation embeddings supplies the objective in Latent Policy Barrier, where dynamics learned from expert data and policy roll-outs guide action denoising through predicted future embeddings [ 12 ] . Predicted future state values provide another criterion: Cosmos Policy learns action, state, and value predictions by fine-tuning a video model, and uses these values to select action proposals in its planning mode [ 13 ] . Feedback can instead operate across network depth, as in WA-LQR, which locally linearizes diffusion Transformer blocks to track contrastive robustness feature targets [ 14 ] . For DHS, the correction reference is the fitted distribution of expert hidden states: coordinate variances determine the attenuation directly, without future state prediction or contrastive feature tracking. IV Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering IV-A Empirical Geometry of Expert Hidden States Studies of image classifiers and Transformers have reported evidence of low-dimensional manifold structure in hidden representations [ 8 , 9 ] . Motivated by these findings, we examine whether the expert hidden-state distribution from an IL robot policy is concentrated in relatively few dimensions and whether regional linear subspaces differ in orientation. We select the Square manipulation task from Robomimic [ 15 ] as a representative task and use a Transformer policy trained by behavior cloning (BC-Transformer). We analyze the approximately 27,000 expert hidden states that form ℋ E \mathcal{H}_{E} , obtained by replaying the original training demonstrations through the frozen policy. To quantify variance concentration, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the mean-centered states. We compute the cumulative explained variance as the sum of the leading covariance eigenvalues divided by the sum of all eigenvalues. Using the 90 % 90\% explained variance criterion employed in prior work [ 8 ] , we find that 29 principal components suffice in the ambient 512 dimensional space. Thus, most observed expert variation can be captured by a low-dimensional linear subspace. For a curved manifold, local tangent subspaces can change orientation relative to the fixed coordinate axes of the hidden-state space. To examine this possibility, we partition the same states into eight clusters using k k -means and fit a rank-29 PCA subspace within each cluster, using these regional subspaces as empirical proxies for local tangent subspaces. We compare every pair of PCA subspaces using principal angles, computed as the inverse cosines of the singular values of the matrix of inner products between their orthonormal basis vectors. Each pair yields 29 principal angles; all are zero for identical subspaces, while larger angles indicate greater differences in orientation. Averaging all 29 principal angles over all 28 cluster pairs gives 44.7 ∘ 44.7^{\circ} , indicating differences in the orientations of the fitted regional subspaces. Together, the variance concentration and regional orientation differences support a low-dimensional manifold-like view of expert hidden-state geometry. These observations therefore motivate the use of a nonlinear chart that allows coordinate rescaling to act along location-dependent directions in hidden-state space. This separates policy training from the design of the steering update, without requiring additional expert action targets. The expert hidden-state density does not uniquely determine the update: different chart scales can describe the same density while yielding different DHS updates at a fixed β > 0 \beta>0 (Appendix A-C ). Chart learning and regularization therefore help define the steering rule, in addition to fitting the expert distribution. VI-B Limitations DHS fits the distribution of expert hidden states, including their observation history information, without modeling temporal transitions. A hidden-state can be compatible with the fitted distribution yet inappropriate for the current task phase or a successful continuation. Combining expert geometry with predictions of an intervention’s future consequences is a natural extension, connecting hidden-state steering with predictive guidance [ 12 , 13 ] . The evaluation covers fixed BC-Transformer checkpoints with low-dimensional observations in simulation, and a single intervention site. In Table I , DHS reduces clean Transport success from 45.0 % 45.0\% to 36.0 % 36.0\% , and adding Action EWMA to DHS lowers noisy success on Can and Coffee-D1. The fitted geometry depends on preprocessing and chart regularization; its coordinate statistics provide a steering reference rather than a model of task error. Future work could also combine DHS with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection to adapt when and how strongly steering should be applied based on departures from the expert hidden-state distribution. VII Conclusion DHS uses expert hidden-state geometry to improve the robustness of frozen IL policies at test time. Motivated by the low-dimensional manifold-like geometry of expert hidden states, its central idea is to apply variance-dependent rescaling in nonlinear coordinates to produce location-dependent steering directions. We use SPRG-based chart learning to fit expert coordinates and their variances. DHS improves mean success over the unmodified policy across four simulated manipulation tasks under observation noise. On Square, the learned coordinate construction yields higher mean success than linear PCA coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. The strength sweep further shows that stronger coordinate attenuation does not necessarily improve execution. Together with the gains over unmodified policies and the benefits alongside Action EWMA on Square and Transport, these results establish expert hidden states as a useful reference for selective test-time steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining.
